analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate tobacco products, restrict their marketing and advertising, and ban broadcast cigarette ads.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to a House subcommittee on March 22, 2001, it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, despite 52 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give the Food and Drug Administration legal authority over tobacco products, something the industry had fought for decades. It would make the FDA's 1996 youth-marketing rules legally valid, order new restrictions on tobacco marketing and advertising modeled on the 1997 tobacco settlement, ban tobacco ads on broadcast media, require accurate health warnings, and cut federal funds to states that fail to run real tobacco-control programs, including retailer licensing and underage-sales enforcement. It died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teens, who would face fewer legal channels to buy cigarettes and less targeted tobacco marketing; smokers, who would get stronger, rotating health warnings and could not be told a product is 'reduced risk' unless the FDA verified it; and the general public, through state tobacco-control programs funded and enforced with federal conditions.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds nicotine and tobacco products to the definitions of 'drug' and 'device' under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, giving the FDA clear jurisdiction over tobacco for the first time by statute.
It declares the FDA's 1996 tobacco regulations lawful and sets them to take effect one year after enactment, reviving rules that restricted tobacco sales and advertising aimed at young people.

It requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to add the marketing, advertising, and access restrictions from the 1997 tobacco settlement's Proposed Resolution, promulgate stronger rotating health warnings for cigarettes and smokeless tobacco, and make it unlawful to advertise tobacco on any medium regulated by the FCC.
It bars manufacturers from claiming a tobacco product is 'reduced risk' unless the Secretary has determined it actually presents a significantly reduced risk to health.

It requires states to adopt a model tobacco-control program — retailer licensing, compliance inspections, penalties, and performance goals — or lose up to 20 percent of their federal tobacco-control funds, with a federal licensing backstop and coverage of tribal retailers.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who would lose unrestricted ability to market and advertise, including a total ban on broadcast tobacco advertising; tobacco retailers, who would face state licensing, inspections, and penalties for selling to minors; and broadcasters and the advertising industry, which would lose tobacco ad revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill adopts the tobacco settlement's Proposed Resolution as its regulatory template rather than writing independent FDA rules, and it instructs the Secretary to exclude any marketing restriction that would violate the First Amendment — terms originally negotiated with the tobacco manufacturers themselves, which could limit how far the regulation could go.

While the bill generally allows states to impose stricter tobacco rules than the federal government, it preempts states from requiring any health-related statements on tobacco packages or ads beyond the federally required warnings.
Retailer licensing, compliance inspections, and enforcement create real administrative costs for small stores that sell tobacco and for state and federal agencies that must run the programs.

The ban on tobacco advertising on FCC-regulated media raises free-speech objections that courts would likely have tested, and the bill itself acknowledges the First Amendment could block some marketing restrictions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health gains — an enforceable federal regime over tobacco marketing, sales to minors, and health claims — are large and well-targeted at the leading preventable cause of death. The main costs fall on the tobacco industry and on retailers in the form of compliance burdens, and the design concessions (settlement-based terms, a First Amendment carve-out, warning preemption) make the bill more modest than a fully independent FDA framework would have been. On balance it is a strong public-health bill with real but narrow costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee in March 2001, and no further action was ever taken on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on March 15, 2001, joined by 38 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On March 22, 2001, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
The bill accumulated 52 cosponsors — 49 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 107th Congress.
Because the Congress ended on January 3, 2003, the bill died without a vote and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: no FDA jurisdiction over tobacco was enacted, so cigarette marketing, advertising, and 'reduced risk' claims remained unregulated at the federal level. Broadcasters and the advertising industry also kept tobacco ad revenue.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FDA Tobacco Jurisdiction Act and recruited 38 original cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee referred the bill to the Health Subcommittee and never took it up; no hearing, markup, or vote occurred under his chairmanship.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry had spent years in court and Congress opposing FDA jurisdiction over tobacco, including a successful Supreme Court challenge to the very 1996 rule this bill would have validated.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic: 49 of 208 House Democrats cosponsored versus 3 of 223 House Republicans, and the bill originated with a Democratic sponsor [S4].

industries.note: The bill would give the FDA jurisdiction over tobacco, validate the 1996 youth-marketing rules, restrict advertising and promotion, require stronger warnings, and police 'reduced risk' claims — all of which cut into an industry whose profits depend on recruiting new smokers. Its gain from the bill's death was the continuation of an unregulated market.
The bill makes it unlawful to advertise tobacco products on any medium of electronic communication regulated by the FCC, eliminating tobacco ad revenue for broadcasters and agencies.

industries.industry: Tobacco retailers (convenience and other small stores)
industries.note: Retailers would face state licensing, mandatory compliance inspections, penalties including license suspension, and possible federal licensing — real compliance costs — though the rules target underage sales rather than the core business of adult sales.
